What is meant by long format data and wide format data? Which do we generally prefer for statistical analysis?

Long format data refers to multiple rows for each observational unit (e.g. recurring ID numbers for test scores such as math/reading)–this is generally the preferred format for statistical analysis because it is expected by many R functions from visualization libraries (ggplot2) to statistical modeling functions (lm/ANOVA/mixed effects models).
Wide format data generally has one row for each observational unit with different measurements separated by columns (e.g. one ID number followed by a math column and a reading column).


Task 2: Note: Use Chaining where possible!


Glass data

#Importing glass data to glass variable
glass <- read.table(
  "https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/glass.data",
  sep = ",",
  header = FALSE
  )
names(glass) <- c(
  "ID", "RI", "Na", "Mg", "Al", "Si", "K", "Ca", "Ba", "Fe", "Type_of_glass"
)


Start a chain on your data object that overwrites the Type_of_glass variable using mutate().


glass_filtered <- glass |>
  #Map numeric codes to descriptive character factors using all 7 defined levels
  mutate(
    Type_of_glass = factor(
      Type_of_glass,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
      labels = c(
      "building_windows_float_processed",
      "building_windows_non_float_processed",
      "vehicle_windows_float_processed",
      "vehicle_windows_non_float_processed",
      "containers",
      "tableware",
      "headlamps"
      )
    )
  )


Continue your chain and keep only observations where the Fe variable is less than 0.2 and the Type of Glass is either “tableware” or “headlamp”.


glass_filtered <- glass |>
  mutate(
    Type_of_glass = factor(
      Type_of_glass,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
      labels = c(
      "building_windows_float_processed",
      "building_windows_non_float_processed",
      "vehicle_windows_float_processed",
      "vehicle_windows_non_float_processed",
      "containers",
      "tableware",
      "headlamps"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  #Keep only low-iron observations for tableware and headlamp types
  filter(
    Fe < 0.2,
    Type_of_glass %in% c("tableware", "headlamps")
  )



Yeast data

yeast <- read.table("https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/yeast.data", 
  header = FALSE, 
  col.names = c("seq_name", "mcg", "gvh", "alm", "mit", "erl", "pox", "vac", "nuc", "class")
)


Start a chain that removes the seq_name and nuc columns.


yeast_summary <- yeast |>
  #Remove identifier columns
  select(-seq_name, -nuc)


Continue your chain to add columns corresponding to the mean and median of each numeric variable (mcg, gvh, alm, mit, erl, pox, and vac) at each class grouping (see the across() function)


yeast_summary <- yeast |>
  #Remove identifier columns
  select(-seq_name, -nuc) |>
  #Group by class to calculate statistics per category
  group_by(class) |>
  #Compute mean/median across all numeric columns
  mutate(
    across(
      c(mcg, gvh, alm, mit, erl, pox, vac),
      list(
        mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        median = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      )
    )
  )

Continue your chain to now sort the data from highest quality to lowest.

  filter(
    quality > 6.5, alcohol < 132

  arrange(desc(quality))


Continue your chain to select only the variables that contain acid, the alochol variable, the type variable and the quality variable.

  filter(
    quality > 6.5, alcohol < 132
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(quality)) |>
  select(
    contains("acid"), alcohol, type, quality
  )


Continue your chain to add the mean and standard deviation of the alcohol variable to the data set for each setting of the quality variable.


wine_summary <- wine |>
  #Filter for high quality ratings and remove extreme outliers
  filter(
    quality > 6.5, alcohol < 132
  ) |>
  #Order quality from highest to lowest
  arrange(desc(quality)) |>
  #Select acid-related variables along with key wine attributes
  select(
    contains("acid"), alcohol, type, quality
  ) |>
  #Group by quality tier to calculate alcohol summary statistics
  group_by(quality) |>
  mutate(
    mean_alcohol = mean(alcohol, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_alcohol = sd(alcohol, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

    playerID, G, W, L

  #Group by manager to aggregate career totals in the database

    G_managed = sum(G, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_W = sum(W, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_L = sum(L, na.rm = TRUE)

#Query NewsAPI and return the article data frame
query_news <- function(subject, from_date, api_key) {

  response <- GET(
    url = "https://newsapi.org/v2/everything",
    query = list(
      q = subject,
      from = from_date,
      language = "en",
      pageSize = 50,
      apiKey = api_key
    )
  )
  #Parse JSON response
  parsed_response <- content(
    response,
    as = "parsed",
    simplifyVector = TRUE
  )
  as_tibble(parsed_response$articles)
}

# 1. Separate weekdays and weekends
add_day_type <- function(df) {
  df |>
    mutate(
      day_type = factor(if_else(wday(date) %in% c(1,7), "Weekend", "Weekday"))
    )
}

test_prep <- add_day_type(test_raw)

# 2. Extract training means and sds
train_means <- sapply(train_prep[num_cols], mean)
train_sds <- sapply(train_prep[num_cols], sd)

# 3. Standardize training set

train_std[num_cols] <- scale(train_prep[num_cols], center = train_means, scale = train_sds)

# 4. Standardize test set using training parameters
test_std <- test_prep
for (col in num_cols) {

\[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}} \sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{test}}} (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}\]

calc_rmse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
}

)

seasons *holiday

  data = train_std
)

  bike_count ~ temp + humidity + wind_speed + visibility + dew_point_temp + solar_radiation + rainfall + snowfall + seasons + holiday + day_type + seasons:holiday + seasons:temp + temp:rainfall + I(temp^2) + I(humidity^2),
  data = train_std
)

rmse_m3 <- calc_rmse(test_std$bike_count, pred_m3)

##Splitting the Data
Before officially fitting any models, we’ll split our data into a training and testing set:

bikes_split <- rsample::initial_split(new_bikes_data,prop=0.75,strata=season)
bikes_train=training(bikes_split)
bikes_test=testing(bikes_split)

##Fitting MLR Models
We’ll make one more modification to the data set by creating a binary type factor variable for the date that’s based on where it falls on a weekend or not.

#Converting date variable into binary type of categorical variable
updated_bikes_data <- new_bikes_data |>
  mutate(type_of_day = factor(ifelse(wday(date) %in% c(1,7), "Weekend","Weekday")))

new_bikes_train = bikes_train |>
  mutate(type_of_day = factor(ifelse(wday(date) %in% c(1,7), "Weekend","Weekday")))
new_bikes_test = bikes_test |>
  mutate(type_of_day = factor(ifelse(wday(date) %in% c(1,7), "Weekend","Weekday")))

#Isolate numeric variables for standardizing
numvars_one <- sapply(new_bikes_train,is.numeric)
numvars_two <- sapply(new_bikes_test,is.numeric)
numvars_all <- sapply(updated_bikes_data,is.numeric)

Note that several columns were isolated so we can standardize the numerical variables.

#Standardizing numeric variables for training set
scaled_bikes_train <- new_bikes_train
scaled_bikes_train[numvars_one] <- scale(new_bikes_train[numvars_one])

#Collecting the mean and sd vectors from the training set  
scaled_bikes_train_means <- sapply(scaled_bikes_train[numvars_one],mean)
scaled_bikes_train_sds <- sapply(scaled_bikes_train[numvars_one],sd)

#Same standardizing procedure for testing set, but with the mean and sd of the training set
scaled_bikes_test <- new_bikes_test
scaled_bikes_test[numvars_two] <- scale(new_bikes_test[numvars_two],center=scaled_bikes_train_means,scale=scaled_bikes_train_sds)

With our data sets scaled, we can fit three type of MLR models using the scaled training set:

an additive MLR model with all the predictors (numerical and categorical)
the same additive MLR model with all predictors plus a few interaction terms
the model from part (ii) along with a couple of quadratic terms

mod3 = lm(count~temperature+humidity+rainfall+snowfall+windspeed+visibility+dewpoint+radiation+season+holiday+type_of_day+season:holiday+season:temperature+temperature:rainfall+I(temperature^2)+I(humidity^2),data=as.data.frame(scaled_bikes_train))
